segments.t: korTTY can color words and patterns in terminal output as it arrives — errors in red, warnings underlined, IP and MAC addresses, interface names and link states on network devices — so the lines that matter stand out while output scrolls by. Highlighting only changes how the text looks: what the server sent, what you copy, the terminal log and what the AI features read stay exactly the same.

Highlighting is off until you switch it on, for one pane with a menu or the shortcut, for every terminal of a connection with the KTPH000connection's rule setKTPH001, or for every pane with a KTPH002default rule setKTPH003. Each terminal pane shows at most one KTPH004rule setKTPH005 at a time. korTTY ships three built-in sets, and you can create KTPH006your ownKTPH007.

KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, KTPH008, KTPH009 and KTPH010 in bold red; exception class names such as KTPH011 or KTPH012 in red; KTPH013, KTPH014 and KTPH015 underlined in yellow. Words match whole and in any case, so KTPH016 is marked but KTPH017 is not.

IPv4 addresses with an optional prefix length (KTPH000), IPv6 addresses including compressed forms (KTPH001), and MAC addresses with colons, dashes or in Cisco's dotted form (KTPH002), all underlined. Numbers that only look like an address, such as KTPH003, are left alone.

Link and session states on switches and routers: KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004 and similar in bold red, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007 and KTPH008 in bold green, and interface names as Cisco, Arista and Juniper print them (KTPH009, KTPH010, KTPH011, KTPH012, KTPH013) underlined in cyan.

The built-in sets use the theme's ANSI colors, so they follow your color settings and the colors of each connection. Every rule also makes its text bold or underlined, so a match still stands out for color-blind users and in a monochrome theme.

Highlighting works per pane: in a split tab every pane can show a different set, and a new split takes over a set chosen for the pane it was split from; without such a choice it follows its own connection.

KTPH006KeyboardKTPH007: KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013 (KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 on macOS) switches highlighting on or off for the pane that has the keyboard focus. Switching it back on brings back the set that pane showed last; a pane that never showed one starts with its connection's rule set or the default rule set, or with KTPH020Errors and warningsKTPH021 when there is neither. The status bar names the set that is now on.
KTPH000View → HighlightingKTPH001: KTPH002Highlighting OnKTPH003 does the same as the shortcut. Below it, pick KTPH004NoneKTPH005 or a rule set for the focused pane of the active tab.

KTPH000Terminal context menuKTPH001: right-click a pane and open KTPH002HighlightingKTPH003 for the same entries, applied to the pane you clicked. The submenu is there even when terminal effects are switched off.
Both menus list your own rule sets below the built-in ones and end with KTPH000Manage Rule Sets…KTPH001, which opens the KTPH002rule-set editorKTPH003 on the set the pane shows.

A set you choose in these menus or with the shortcut applies to the running session only and is not saved: the next tab you open for the same connection starts with the KTPH000connection's rule setKTPH001 or, if it has none, the default rule set, which is KTPH002NoneKTPH003 unless you chose one in the settings. To keep a set for a connection, choose it in the connection editor. This differs from KTPH004View → Terminal EffectKTPH005, which stores the effect on the connection.

The shortcut also works while the menu bar is hidden and in terminal-only fullscreen. On Windows and Linux korTTY keeps KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 for itself, so it does not reach the program in the terminal; plain KTPH011KTPH003KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH004KTPH014 still reaches the shell as backspace.

The KTPH000Keyword highlightingKTPH001 section of KTPH002Configuration → Global Settings → TerminalKTPH003 holds three settings that apply to every pane; see KTPH004Terminal settingsKTPH005 for the details.
The master switch. Off means no pane is highlighted, whatever was chosen anywhere; the highlighting menus are greyed out and the shortcut only shows a note in the status bar.
KTPH000Also highlight in full-screen programs (vim, less, htop)KTPH001
Highlights inside programs that use the alternate screen as well.
The set every pane shows unless its connection or the pane has a set of its own. Choose a set here to have highlighting on in every new and open terminal.
A pane shows the first of these that applies:
the set chosen for that pane in a menu or with the shortcut, including KTPH000NoneKTPH001;
the KTPH000connection's rule setKTPH001, including KTPH002NoneKTPH003;

A rule set that no longer exists is skipped, so the next level decides. Saving the settings moves every open pane to the set it now resolves to, so a new default appears at once in every pane whose connection and pane have no choice of their own.

A connection can have a rule set of its own, for example KTPH000Network devicesKTPH001 for your switches and routers and KTPH002Errors and warningsKTPH003 for application servers. Open the connection in the Connection Manager, switch to the KTPH004Terminal SettingsKTPH005 tab and pick the set under KTPH006Keyword highlightingKTPH007 in the KTPH008Terminal behaviorKTPH009 section:
The KTPH000default rule setKTPH001; the entry names the set the default shows now. New and existing connections start with this choice.
No highlighting, whatever the default rule set is.
A built-in set or one of your own
That set, in every pane of the connection.

The section applies whether or not the connection uses its own terminal settings, and it stays when terminal effects are switched off. While the master switch in KTPH000Settings → TerminalKTPH001 is off, the section says so and no set shows.

Saving in the Connection Manager moves the open panes of that connection, in every window, to the new set at once. A pane with a set chosen in a menu or with the shortcut keeps that choice until you change it there.

Tabs opened from the saved connection through Quick Connect, KTPH000DuplicateKTPH001 or a KTPH002projectKTPH003 use its set. A pane opened with KTPH004Split Right (new connection)KTPH005 or KTPH006Split Down (new connection)KTPH007 follows the connection it was opened to, unless it took over a set chosen for the pane it was split from.

The choice is stored with the connection in KTPH000 and survives duplicating, exporting and importing; an export carries only the id of the set, never its rules. A set that no longer exists — because you deleted it, or because the connection was exported on another computer or comes from a shared KTPH001teamworkKTPH002 file — is shown as KTPH003Missing rule setKTPH004 in the dropdown, and the connection's panes follow the default rule set until you pick another one. The built-in sets have the same id on every computer.

The rule-set editor creates and changes your own rule sets. Open it with KTPH000View → Highlighting → Manage Rule Sets…KTPH001, with KTPH002Manage Rule Sets…KTPH003 in a pane's KTPH004HighlightingKTPH005 context submenu, or with KTPH006Edit Rules…KTPH007 next to the default rule set in KTPH008Configuration → Global Settings → TerminalKTPH009.

KTPH000Rule setsKTPH001 on the left lists the built-in sets, marked KTPH002built-inKTPH003, and then yours. The built-in sets are read-only, but you can select one to read its patterns. KTPH004DuplicateKTPH005 copies the selected set, built-in or your own, into a new set you can change; KTPH006NewKTPH007 starts an empty set with one rule to fill in, and KTPH008DeleteKTPH009 removes one of your sets.
KTPH000Rule set nameKTPH001 is the name the menus and the default rule set dropdown show.

KTPH000RulesKTPH001 lists the set's rules in priority order: where two rules match the same text, the upper rule wins, as in the built-in sets. Use ▲ and ▼ to change the order, KTPH002Add RuleKTPH003 to add a rule below the selected one and KTPH004Remove RuleKTPH005 to delete it. KTPH006OnKTPH007 switches a rule off without deleting it. KTPH008PatternKTPH009 shows each pattern in the look it gives, KTPH010Applies toKTPH011 whether it colors the matched text or the whole line, KTPH012HitsKTPH013 how many places it highlights in the test text below, and KTPH014CheckKTPH015 whether something is wrong with it.

Below the table you edit the selected rule. KTPH003PatternKTPH004 is a word or phrase to find, or a Java regular expression when KTPH005Regular expressionKTPH006 is on. KTPH007Ignore caseKTPH008 matches upper and lower case alike, and KTPH009Whole wordKTPH010 only matches where the hit is not part of a longer word, so KTPH000 marks KTPH001 but not KTPH002. KTPH011Applies toKTPH012 colors either the KTPH013Matched textKTPH014 or the KTPH015Whole lineKTPH016, soft-wrapped rows included.

KTPH000Text colorKTPH001 and KTPH002BackgroundKTPH003 are KTPH004UnchangedKTPH005 (the program's own color), one of the 16 theme colors, or KTPH006CustomKTPH007 with a color picker. Theme colors follow your color settings and the colors of each connection, like the built-in sets; a custom color stays the same everywhere. KTPH008StyleKTPH009 adds KTPH010BoldKTPH011, KTPH012ItalicKTPH013 or KTPH014UnderlineKTPH015. A rule needs at least one color or style.

The KTPH000Test textKTPH001 at the bottom starts with sample log and network-device lines; replace it with output of your own. KTPH002PreviewKTPH003 shows it the way a terminal pane would, using the same matching, the same rule order and the same time limit, and it follows every change as you type. The editor keeps your test text until korTTY quits; it is not saved.

KTPH001CheckKTPH002 says KTPH003InvalidKTPH004 for a rule that cannot work, KTPH005OffKTPH006 for a rule you switched off, KTPH007SlowKTPH008 for a rule that needed more than half of its time limit on a line of the test text, and KTPH009Too slowKTPH010 for a rule that ran out of time there and highlights nothing on that line; a terminal pane switches such a rule off once it has run out of time on three lines (see KTPH011LimitsKTPH012). Hover over the word, or select the rule, for the explanation. While any rule or set has a problem, KTPH013OKKTPH014 is disabled and the line above the buttons names the first one, for example a missing pattern, a regular expression that does not compile, or a pattern such as KTPH000 that also matches empty text.

KTPH001OKKTPH002 saves your rule sets to KTPH000 at once and moves every open pane to its updated set; KTPH003CancelKTPH004 discards all changes. Deleting the set that is your default rule set sets the default back to KTPH005NoneKTPH006. A pane that showed a deleted set falls back to the next level: its connection's rule set, else the default rule set.
To adapt a built-in set, select it, click KTPH000DuplicateKTPH001 and change the copy. The built-in sets themselves stay as korTTY ships them, so a later version can improve their patterns.
New output is highlighted a moment after it appears (about 50 ms), on a background thread, so a fast KTPH000 or a log tail keeps its speed.
A match can continue across a soft-wrapped line, and patterns match wide characters such as CJK text and emoji.
Choosing another set, or KTPH000NoneKTPH001, re-colors the screen at once and the scrollback progressively, newest lines first. KTPH002NoneKTPH003 restores the original colors everywhere.

Full-screen programs such as KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002 are not highlighted unless you allow it in the KTPH003settingsKTPH004: they redraw constantly and bring their own colors, so highlights would flicker and fight them.
When output floods in faster than it can be checked, lines more than 10,000 rows above the bottom are left as they are.
Text a program marks as concealed stays hidden, and links keep their own style.
Highlights also show on connections whose terminal colors are switched off, and they appear in KTPH000terminal recordingsKTPH001, because they are part of what the pane shows.

While the find bar shows results, korTTY waits with re-coloring the scrollback after you switch sets, so the matches you are looking at stay marked. A line that is highlighted while the find bar is open can lose its find mark; search again to bring it back.

Each rule gets at most 2 ms per line of output. A rule that runs out of time three times — usually a regular expression that backtracks badly — is switched off for that pane until you choose a set again. A line, soft-wrapped rows included, is checked up to its first 8,192 characters. The editor's KTPH000CheckKTPH001 column warns about slow rules before they reach a terminal.
You can create up to 32 rule sets with up to 64 rules each, and a pattern can be up to 512 characters long.

A highlight is not a trust signal. The server decides what it prints, so it can print text that matches a rule, just as it can color its own output. Highlighting never changes what is sent or received.

Rule sets stay on your computer, in KTPH000 (see KTPH001Configuration filesKTPH002), and the log names rules and sets by their ids only, never by their patterns or by the text they matched. If you allowed KTPH003anonymous usage statisticsKTPH004, korTTY reports which built-in set was switched on (any set of your own counts only as "custom") and whether that happened from a menu, with the shortcut, through the connection's rule set or through the default rule set, and which of the three settings you changed, with the default rule set again reported only as a built-in set, "custom" or "none" — never patterns, set names or terminal text.
